idiom_name: struct per domain concept + row structs + map_* functions in a repository module
implementation_notes: C has no classes to protect, so the separation is a naming and module discipline: each domain concept gets its own struct plus free functions that carry the behaviour and return error codes, while the table shape lives in separate row structs owned by the persistence module (src/db/*.c). Hand-written map_order_from_row()/map_order_to_params() functions do the translation and call value constructors (money_from_cents, order_validate) instead of copying fields blindly; the SQLite C API - sqlite3_prepare_v2, sqlite3_bind_*, sqlite3_column_* - is only ever touched inside that module. There is no framework equivalent to replace the classic Mapper, so the classic structure (a mapper per aggregate plus a repository) is exactly what you hand-write; it stays justified because the compiler cannot stop anyone from embedding storage columns in a domain struct.
pitfalls: Ownership at the boundary: strings copied out of sqlite3_column_text() must be duplicated and freed by a documented owner, or the domain ends up holding memory owned by the statement.
Nothing enforces the seam: 'just add a column to the struct' erodes the separation silently, so it survives only through module layout, naming and review.
Error codes are easy to ignore - a failed mapping that returns SQLITE_MISMATCH and a partially filled domain struct is the C equivalent of an unvalidated rehydration.
